topic: Infantile amnesia: why we can't remember being a baby
hook: Why you can't remember being a baby
caption:
Your brain was recording from your very first year. A 2025 Yale study scanned babies and found their hippocampus already storing new memories. So why can almost none of us remember being a baby?

One leading theory: the infant brain grows new neurons so fast that old memory links get scrambled. In mice, scientists even brought 'lost' infant memories back using light. So yours may still be in there somewhere.

What's your earliest memory, and how old were you? 👇

Your brain was recording from your very first year. A 2025 Yale study scanned babies and found their hippocampus already storing new memories. So why can almost none of us remember being a baby?

One leading theory: the infant brain grows new neurons so fast that old memory links get scrambled. In mice, scientists even brought 'lost' infant memories back using light. So yours may still be in there somewhere.

What's your earliest memory, and how old were you? 👇

Cover: Why you can't remember being a baby
📷 Paul Goyette from Chicago, USA (CC BY-SA 2.0) via wikimedia

1/5 It has a name (Age 3)
Scientists call it infantile amnesia. Most adults' earliest memories date back to around age 3.
📷 Ansel Adams (Public domain) via wikimedia

2/5 Babies do remember (1 yr)
A 2025 Yale brain-scan study found 1-year-olds already storing new memories in the hippocampus.
📷 Raymond F Sekula Jr, Peter J Jannetta, Kenneth F Casey, Edward M Marchan, L Kath (CC BY 2.0) via wikimedia

3/5 Kids forget later (35%)
Kids aged 5 to 7 recall over 60% of events from age 3. By age 8 or 9, it drops to about 35%.
📷 Eugene Field (Public domain) via wikimedia

4/5 Too many new neurons
In young mice, a burst of new brain cells in the hippocampus wiped out early memories. Babies may be similar.
📷 ZEISS Microscopy from Germany (CC BY 2.0) via wikimedia

5/5 Locked, not deleted?
Scientists brought back 'forgotten' infant memories in mice using light. Yours may still be in there.
📷 Rama (CC BY-SA 2.0 fr) via wikimedia
